title: T3 — Terraform modules
bodyMarkdown:
## Terraform modules

Exam group **5**. Group 4 covered what you write inside one configuration, including `variable`, `output` and `locals` blocks. This group is about packaging that configuration so other configurations can reuse it: where a module's code comes from, what crosses the boundary between a calling module and the module it calls, how a `module` block is used, and how module versions are pinned. Vocabulary: a module is a folder of `.tf` files; the directory you run Terraform in is the root module, and any module it calls with a `module` block is a child module. The name after `module` in that block is its label.

### tf.004.5a — Explain how Terraform sources modules

Every `module` block has a `source` argument, and "The source argument specifies where Terraform retrieves the module source code." The shape of that string, not a separate setting, tells Terraform what kind of location it is: "Terraform can load modules from multiple sources, including the local file system, a Terraform registry, and VCS repositories." Learn the shapes side by side, because the exam hands you a string and asks what kind of source it is.

- **Local path:** begins with `./` or `../`, for example `./modules/network`. The docs say to "Use the ./ or ../ prefix followed by the path to local module source code" for files already on disk.
- **Terraform registry:** three parts, `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`, for example `hashicorp/consul/aws`. A private registry in HCP Terraform adds a hostname in front: `app.terraform.io/<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`.
- **GitHub:** `github.com/<ORGANIZATION>/<MODULE-FOLDER>` over HTTPS, or `git@github.com:<ORGANIZATION>/<MODULE-FOLDER>` over SSH.
- **Any other Git repository:** the `git::` prefix followed by a Git URL, for example `git::https://example.com/vpc.git`. Bitbucket uses a `bitbucket.org/` prefix, and Mercurial uses `hg::`.
- **Archives and object storage:** an HTTPS URL (one ending in an archive extension such as `.zip` is used directly as the archive: "If an HTTPS URL has a common file extension associated with an archive file format, Terraform bypasses the terraform-get=1 redirection"), `s3::` for an S3 bucket object, or `gcs::` for a Google Cloud Storage object. For S3 the docs say "The object stored in the S3 bucket must be an archive with one of the following extensions", such as `.zip` or `.tar.gz`.

Git-based sources can select a revision with the `ref` query parameter, for example `git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0`. It "Specifies a branch name, full or short SHA-1 hash, or tag name to clone." Leave it off and nothing is selected for you: "Terraform defaults to the default branch referenced by HEAD in the repository." So an unpinned Git source follows the repository's default branch.

A repository or archive is called a package, and the module you want may live in a folder inside it. Mark that folder with a double slash: `git::https://example.com/network.git//modules/vpc`, or `hashicorp/consul/aws//modules/consul-cluster` for a registry module. Query parameters go after the subdirectory, as in `git::https://example.com/network.git//modules/vpc?ref=v1.2.0`. Terraform still downloads the whole package: "Terraform extracts the entire package to local disk, but reads the module from the subdirectory."

Sourcing happens at install time, not at plan time. "You must run terraform init after modifying the source argument so that Terraform can update the local code." The same address can be reused: "You can specify the same source address in two or more separate module blocks", each under its own label (5c).

**Exam tip:** a string starting with `./` or `../` is a local path; `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>` is a registry module; a `git::` prefix, `github.com/` or `bitbucket.org/` is a version-control source selected with `?ref=`; a `//` inside the address marks a subdirectory of the package.

### tf.004.5b — Describe variable scope within modules

Each module is its own scope. Terraform's own words for a module: "The resources defined in a module form a self-contained group of resources." The documented ways for a value to cross the boundary are an input variable (in) and an output (out); a local crosses only by being passed as an argument.

**Inward: input variables.** A `variable` block is a module's input, and who supplies the value depends on whether the module is the root or a child. For the root module, "you can set variable values using CLI options, environment variables, variable definition files, or through an HCP Terraform workspace." `TF_VAR_` names were covered in 4c; `-var` and `.tfvars` files are the other methods in that list. For a child module: "In child modules, the parent module passes values to child modules as arguments to the module block." So `-var` and `TF_VAR_` set root variables, while a child's variable receives its value from an argument written in the `module` block: `servers = 5` inside `module "servers" { ... }` sets the child's `var.servers`. The docs state the split directly: "Child modules receive their inputs from a parent module as arguments."

**Variable names are scoped per module.** The label after `variable` "must be unique among all variables in the same module." A parent and a child can each declare a variable called `region` without conflict, because they are different modules. A variable cannot use certain reserved names: the label can be "any valid identifier except the following reserved names: source, version, providers, count, for_each, lifecycle, depends_on, or locals."

**Locals do not cross.** 4c said a `locals` block is invisible outside its module. The docs state the rule: "You can access local values in the module where you define them, but not in other modules." They then give the one exception: "you can pass a local value to a child module as an argument." The local itself is still not visible to the child; its current value is handed over as an input argument, which arrives in the child as an ordinary variable.

**Outward: outputs.** A child module returns a value only if it declares an `output` block: "Child modules can expose resource attributes to parent modules." The parent reads it as `module.<CHILD_MODULE_NAME>.<OUTPUT_NAME>`: "Parent modules can access child module outputs using module.<CHILD_MODULE_NAME>.<OUTPUT_NAME> syntax." If the child never declares an output for a value, the parent has no documented way to read it.

The channels are not interchangeable. A variable carries a value into a child, an output carries a value out of a child, and a local carries nothing across a boundary by itself.

**Exam tip:** "a value the parent gives to the child" is an input variable set as an argument in the `module` block; "a value the child gives back" is an `output` read with `module.<name>.<output>`; "a named expression in the caller that the child cannot see" is a `local`, which only crosses as an argument; `-var` and `TF_VAR_` set root module variables, not a child's.

### tf.004.5c — Use modules in configuration

Start with the two roles. "The .tf files in your working directory when you run terraform plan or terraform apply together form the root module." Every module you call from there is a child module: "Modules you configure using module blocks are called child modules." A child can call its own children: "The root module can also call a child module that calls its own nested child module." In most cases the docs recommend against deep nesting: "we strongly recommend keeping the module tree flat, with only one level of child modules", and connecting modules with expressions at the root instead, for example `vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id`. "We call this flat style of module usage module composition".

A `module` block has a label, `source`, optional `version`, and the child's inputs written as arguments:

- `source` is required. The inputs are whatever the module author declared: "The module developer determines which inputs you can specify for the module."
- `version` applies only to registry sources (5d).
- `count` and `for_each` work on a `module` block just as on a resource, and are mutually exclusive. `count`: "Use this argument to state how many instances of a module to provision." `for_each`: "Use this argument to loop through a set of keys so that Terraform provisions similar module instances."
- `depends_on` and `providers` are also accepted on a `module` block.

Reusing one module twice means two `module` blocks with different labels, not the same label twice: "you must use unique labels for each block." The label is also how you reach outputs: "you can use the module.<label>.<output> syntax to reference them". Its shape depends on `count` and `for_each`. With neither, `module.<MODULE NAME>` is an object with one attribute per output. With `for_each`, "If the corresponding module uses for_each then the value will be a map of objects", and with `count` the value is "a list with the requested number of elements".

Using a module is a workflow, not just a block. Add the `module` block, then initialize. `terraform init` is what installs it: "Terraform clones the module source configurations into a hidden subdirectory of the workspace's working directory." The separate `terraform get` command is about modules alone: "Run the terraform get command to download and update modules declared in the root module." The docs say where they land: "The modules are downloaded into a .terraform subdirectory of the current working directory." And the rule: "Don't commit this directory to your version control repository." After `init`, the module is part of the configuration: "Terraform adds the child module's resources to your workspace and manages them as part of the configuration." Installing and provisioning are separate steps. The docs list "Initialize the workspace to install the module." and then "Apply the configuration to provision the module's resources." So `plan` and `apply` work with the modules that `init` has already installed.

After the first install, `init` leaves modules alone. Re-running it "will install the sources for any modules that were added to configuration since the last init", but it "will not change any already-installed modules." Two things update an existing install: `terraform init -upgrade`, which updates "all modules to the latest available source code" (within any `version` constraint on a registry module, 5d), and `terraform get -update`, which checks modules that are already downloaded for updates. Editing `source`, or the `version` of a registry module, always needs a fresh `init` first (5a, 5d).

Two boundary notes for providers, which cross differently from variables. A child module "automatically inherits default provider configurations from its parent." Aliased configurations are not inherited: "Additional provider configurations (those with the alias argument set) are never inherited automatically by child modules", so they must be passed with the `providers` argument. And inheritance covers settings only: "Only provider configurations are inherited by child modules, not provider source or version requirements."

**Exam tip:** "the directory where you run Terraform" is the root module and every `module` block it contains is a child; "download the module code" is `terraform init` (or `terraform get`), into a `.terraform` subdirectory that is never committed; "two copies of the same module with different settings" is two labelled `module` blocks, or one block with `count` or `for_each`; changing a `source` always means running `init` again.

### tf.004.5d — Manage module versions

Version control depends on the source type, and the exam checks that you do not apply the registry's mechanism to the other sources. The `version` argument "only applies when installing modules from a registry", and the docs repeat it: "You can only use the version argument when the source argument points to a module listed in a registry". Two other source kinds have their own answers:

- **Local path:** "Modules sourced from local file paths do not support version", because they are "loaded from the same source repository and always share the same version as their caller."
- **Git and other version-control sources:** no `version` argument. Select a revision with `?ref=`, for example `?ref=v1.2.0` (5a): a tag or a commit SHA fixes the version, while a branch name is accepted too but a branch keeps moving as new commits arrive, so it is not a fixed version.

If you omit `version` for a registry module, the default is the newest available: "Defaults to latest version available from the source". The docs recommend against leaving it open: "We recommend explicitly constraining the acceptable version numbers to avoid unexpected or unwanted changes."

"A version constraint is a string literal containing one or more conditions separated by commas." For example `">= 1.2.0, < 2.0.0"`. The operators to know:

- `=` or no operator: "Allows only one exact version number. Cannot be combined with other conditions." So `version = "6.0.1"` pins that single release.
- `!=`: "Excludes an exact version number."
- `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`: "The > and >= operators request newer versions. The < and <= operators request older versions."
- `~>` allows only the right-most version component to increment. "~> 1.0.4: Allows Terraform to install 1.0.5 and 1.0.10 but not 1.1.0." And "~> 1.1: Allows Terraform to install 1.2 and 1.10 but not 2.0." The number of components you write decides which one may move, so `~> 1.0.4` stays in the 1.0 line while `~> 1.1` stays in major version 1.

When several versions qualify, Terraform picks the newest: "For plugins and modules, Terraform uses the newest installed version that meets the applicable constraints." If none is installed, "it attempts to download the newest version that meets the applicable constraints."

The part that surprises people: the dependency lock file does not cover modules. `.terraform.lock.hcl` records the provider selections you made, and "At present, the dependency lock file tracks only provider dependencies." Its page spells out the consequence for modules: "Terraform does not remember version selections for remote modules". A registry module with a range constraint such as `~> 1.1` can therefore move to a newer release the next time Terraform selects a version, and no lock file prevents that: "Terraform will always select the newest available module version that meets the specified version constraints." That happens on a first install, or after `init -upgrade` or `get -update`, not on a repeat `init` of an already-installed module (5c). The documented way to freeze a module is the constraint itself: "You can use an exact version constraint to ensure that Terraform will always select the same module version."

To move forward on purpose, run `terraform init -upgrade` or `terraform get -update` (5c). Plain `init` does not change an installed module. Changing the `version` of a registry module needs a fresh `init`: "You must run terraform init after modifying the version argument so that Terraform can update the local code." For third-party modules the docs recommend an exact version: "Require specific versions to ensure that updates only happen when convenient to you when your infrastructure depends on third-party modules."

**Exam tip:** "`version` on a `./` path or a `git::` source" is the trap, because `version` is registry-only and Git pins with `?ref=`; "which versions does `~> 1.0.4` allow" is 1.0.5 and 1.0.10 but not 1.1.0; "does `.terraform.lock.hcl` pin this module's version" is no, it tracks only providers, so an exact `version` constraint is the pin.

### Warnings

- Do not run `terraform init`, `plan`, `apply` or `destroy` against real cloud credentials in this workbook, and never call `ExecuteTerraformCommand` or `ExecuteTerragruntCommand` from this workbook's tools. A module you install can contain resources that cost money once applied.
- A `version` constraint belongs only on registry modules: the docs say the argument "only applies when installing modules from a registry" and that local-path modules "do not support version". Do not add it to a local path or a `git::` source. Pin a Git source with `?ref=` (a tag or commit) and a registry module with an exact `version`.
- The dependency lock file protects provider versions, not module versions. Treat a module with a range constraint as able to change between installs.
- The documented channels for a module's values are `output` blocks (out) and arguments to its variables (in). Do not rely on a local value or a child's resource address being reachable from the caller.
